routes.description: Establish that classical theism offers a coherent and comparatively adequate explanation of central features of reality and withstands the principal objections raised against it.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if one or more independent theistic inferences remain reasonable under the relevant alternatives and suffering is not shown logically incompatible with classical theism.

motionBridge.description: Connect the surviving explanatory case and the coherence of classical theism to the intellectual reasonableness of personal theistic belief.

centralBridges.description: Show that the universe's contingent existence, beginning, or life-permitting conditions warrant a transcendent or intelligent explanation.
Show that intentional minds and objective moral obligations fit a personal divine foundation better than the proposed naturalistic account.
Show that omnipotence and perfect goodness can coexist with suffering when freedom and morally sufficient purposes constrain feasible worlds.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend explanatory power and other theoretical virtues as rational evidential standards alongside novel prediction.
Support a specifically historical inference to divine action from the evidence offered concerning Jesus's resurrection.

routes.description: Establish that the proposed theistic explanations lack sufficient evidential or conceptual support and that classical divine attributes conflict with the observed extent of suffering.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the central theistic inferences have viable naturalistic alternatives or defective premises and classical theism cannot coherently account for severe suffering.

motionBridge.description: Connect the evidential shortcomings and the unresolved problem of suffering to the conclusion that belief in classical theism is not intellectually reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Provide naturalistic causal or evolutionary alternatives that block the claimed necessity of divine explanations.
Show that invoking God lacks predictive or informative explanatory content sufficient to support the proposed inferences.
Show that an omnipotent and wholly benevolent God is incompatible with severe suffering absent a coherent necessity or greater-good account.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Challenge whether ancient testimony can discriminate resurrection from unreliable or analogous miracle claims.
Challenge divine-command and divine-nature accounts as foundations for objective moral standards.

sections.title: Cosmic Origin and Causal Explanation
sections.rationale: The need for an explanation of the universe and the status of quantum counterexamples determine whether a central inference to a transcendent personal cause can proceed.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning and Explanatory Standards
sections.rationale: The comparative treatment of design, chance, physical necessity, and predictive power governs whether cosmic fine-tuning provides rational support for theism.

sections.title: Intentionality and Scientific Naturalism
sections.rationale: Whether naturalism can coherently account for intentional thought and whether science entails the disputed philosophical consequences bears on the comparative reasonableness of the two worldviews.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: The debate over whether objective value and obligation require God supplies an independent route to theism and a central naturalistic challenge to that route.

sections.title: Resurrection and Testimonial Evidence
sections.rationale: The reliability and comparative force of the offered historical evidence determine whether the specifically Christian resurrection inference contributes to the case for God.

sections.title: Divine Goodness, Freedom, and Suffering
sections.rationale: The compatibility of extensive human and animal suffering with omnipotence and perfect goodness directly controls whether classical theism remains coherent and reasonable.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A contingent universe with a finite beginning is best explained by a transcendent, immaterial, personal creator.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Craig, and the uninterrupted opening statement remains attributed to him throughout this span.

response.rationale: This constructive supplies a central explanatory route from contingency and a finite beginning to a transcendent personal cause.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The constructive is direct and organized, but the personal-cause bridge remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is recoverable, though the shift from transcendent explanation to personal being needs a clearer definition and bridge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evidence is described probabilistically, but the personal-creator conclusion is stronger than the excerpted support establishes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The contingent-explanation structure is intelligible, but personality does not follow without a material additional bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The finite-beginning claim receives asserted evidential support, while contingency and personal causation remain substantially compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly advances the central cosmic-explanation bridge and is indispensable to that route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected constructive does not develop a sufficiently specific rival interpretation for a meaningful charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states a contingency argument, claims strong evidence for a finite beginning, and identifies the explanation as a transcendent personal being.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by design than by physical necessity or chance.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage occurs within Craig's explicitly introduced and uninterrupted opening statement, with numbered transitions identifying his arguments.

response.rationale: This constructive compares necessity, chance, and design as explanations of life-permitting cosmic conditions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely develops the selected central inference, though the comparative design warrant is incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternatives and intended comparative conclusion are clear, with an implicit qualification about which hypotheses exhaust the live options.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues comparative plausibility rather than certainty, but the excerpt does not fully defend the probability assignment to design.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuning could reflect physical necessity or chance rather than design.
charity.decisiveQualification: Independence from current laws does not by itself exclude deeper necessity, and low probability requires a specified measure and rival priors.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative structure is valid in form, with a bounded but important gap from rejecting two rivals to favoring design.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific features of constants and quantities are invoked, but probability measures, priors, and deeper physical alternatives are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central bridge requiring an intelligent explanation of life-permitting conditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The principal rivals are expressly considered, but their strongest deeper-law and probability-measure qualifications remain underdeveloped.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly contrasts physical necessity, chance, and design, denies necessity from independence of constants, and invokes low chance.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The evident existence of intentional mental states conflicts with materialist atheism's denial of aboutness while fitting a worldview grounded in a divine mind.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig remains the named speaker in his continuous opening statement, and the passage explicitly discusses Rosenberg from Craig's opposing perspective.

response.rationale: This constructive argues that intentional mental states conflict with the stated materialist position and fit a divine-mind worldview.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move clearly states the experiential datum and comparative worldview claim, while leaving explanatory details compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: Intentionality and the target position are identifiable, but the scope shifts between Rosenberg's view, materialism, atheism, and naturalism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the result a reductio of atheism exceeds an argument directed at a particular eliminativist materialism.

charity.alternative: A naturalist may accept intentional discourse through functional, representational, or non-eliminativist accounts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Refuting Rosenberg's eliminativism would not refute every naturalistic or atheistic account of intentionality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The experiential objection to eliminativism is forceful, but the inference from one materialist view to atheism generally is invalid without qualification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Immediate experience supports the existence claim, yet the comparative theistic explanation and exclusion of naturalistic accounts are asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central bridge comparing intentional minds under theistic and naturalistic accounts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly reports Rosenberg's striking denial but generalizes the consequence too broadly to atheism as such.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites Rosenberg's denial of aboutness, appeals to Craig's present thought, calls atheism absurd, and contrasts finite minds under theism.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, with values grounded in God and duties grounded in divine commands.
moves.attributionBasis: The numbered sixth argument appears in the uninterrupted opening statement that the moderator expressly assigned to William Lane Craig.

response.rationale: This constructive offers God and divine commands as foundations for objective moral values and duties.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The argument is explicit and central, but both the moral-realist premise and grounding relation are compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The values-duties distinction and grounding claims are recoverable, though the modal dependence claim has only an implicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that objective morality requires God is not matched by the excerpt's limited comparison with nihilism.

charity.alternative: Secular moral realism may ground objective reasons or values without divine commands.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that one atheistic nihilism lacks moral facts does not exclude all non-theistic realist foundations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The syllogistic form is usable, but the crucial conditional from no God to no objective morality is largely undefended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The existence and divine-dependence premises are asserted in the excerpt without representative moral evidence or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the moral half of the central human-reality bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move contrasts theism with nihilism but does not engage the strongest non-theistic realist alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes values grounded in God from duties grounded in commands and formulates the objective-morality conditional.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' transformed belief are best explained by Jesus's resurrection, which entails God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: This numbered seventh argument remains within Craig's explicitly introduced opening statement and uses his characteristic first-person argumentative framing.

response.rationale: This constructive presents three historical claims as evidence for resurrection and consequently for God's existence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It identifies a clear historical route, but the selected evidence only begins the case and compresses source verification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical inference is clear, with an implicit rather than explicit qualification concerning what majority recognition covers.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames resurrection as a best explanation and personal belief, but the entailment to divine action outruns the excerpted verification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is coherent, but the bridge from the three claims to resurrection rather than alternatives is underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A majority-of-historians assertion and the empty-tomb claim are specific, but source independence and alternative comparison are absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the subsidiary historical-case bridge concerning resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected constructive states the positive case without developing a specific competing historical explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes three facts allegedly recognized by most historians and begins with the post-crucifixion empty-tomb claim.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Pervasive quantum indeterminacy supplies events without sufficient causes and therefore challenges the causal principle used in cosmological arguments.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Rosenberg the floor at event 432, and his continuous opening statement includes direct references to Craig's argument here.

components.text: Contacts the causal premise by offering apparently causeless differences between otherwise indistinguishable radioactive atoms.
Does not separately defeat the contingency-to-personal-explanation bridge for the universe as a whole.

response.rationale: The uranium example directly challenges unrestricted sufficient-cause reasoning, but an event within a physical system does not by itself answer the distinct claim about an absolute cosmic beginning.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive causal premise but leaves the cosmic-scope and personal-explanation components unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterexample is clear, but 'no cause whatsoever' conflates absence of a deterministic sufficient cause with every relevant causal explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical interpretation of quantum mechanics is stronger than the example warrants and omits interpretive qualifications.

charity.alternative: The cosmological premise may concern things beginning to exist from nothing rather than probabilistic transitions in an existing quantum system.
charity.decisiveQualification: Radioactive decay challenges universal sufficient causation but is not straightforwardly analogous to an absolute beginning.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample bears on a universal causal principle, though extending it to cosmic origination requires an additional analogy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Uranium decay is a concrete example, but its metaphysical interpretation is asserted as uniquely dictated by quantum mechanics.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the causal requirement within the central cosmic-explanation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge identifies a serious premise issue but treats the atomic and cosmic cases as more directly parallel than established.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares indistinguishable uranium atoms and asserts that spontaneous alpha emission has no cause, explicitly invoking quantum mechanics.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: The Euthyphro dilemma and alternative ethical theories challenge the claim that objective morality depends on or uniquely indicates God.
moves.attributionBasis: Rosenberg remains the uninterrupted speaker after his explicit introduction, and he directly names and criticizes Craig's objective-values argument.

components.text: Contacts the grounding demand by asking what about God makes imposed norms morally right.
Mentions alternative ethical theories but does not explain how any one grounds objective values and duties.

response.rationale: The Euthyphro-style question directly pressures divine-command grounding, while the invocation of alternatives remains too generic to answer the full comparative case.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It reaches the decisive grounding component but only gestures toward the promised secular alternatives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dilemma and burden question are identifiable, though the relationship among commands, rightness, and God's nature is only implicitly framed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move primarily raises a challenge and notes alternatives rather than claiming that a particular alternative has been established.

charity.alternative: Moral rightness may be grounded in God's essential nature rather than arbitrary decrees.
charity.decisiveQualification: A nature-based account avoids simple voluntarism but still needs to explain why that nature constitutes goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The grounding challenge is logically apt, but merely noting multiple theories does not establish their adequacy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual dilemma needs little empirical support, while the existence and adequacy of alternatives receive no substantive defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly supports the subsidiary burden challenging divine moral grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question reaches the underlying grounding problem, though it initially frames the view too heavily in terms of imposed norms.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks what feature of God explains normative rightness and states that numerous alternative ethical theories exist.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Ancient resurrection testimony is insufficiently reliable to justify a divine miracle, especially when comparable testimony for other religious claims is rejected.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Rosenberg's uninterrupted opening statement and expressly turns to rebut Craig's New Testament argument.

components.text: Contacts testimonial discrimination by comparing Christian miracle reports with other religious claims the audience would reject.
Does not directly assess the empty tomb, appearances, transformed belief, or their source independence.

response.rationale: The analogical challenge attacks selective trust in miracle testimony, but it leaves the specific evidential structure of the resurrection inference largely unexamined.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a material testimonial component without answering the principal historical claims individually.

precisionFindings.rationale: The intended parity challenge is recoverable, though the relevant similarities between the compared testimonial records remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The rhetorical questions appropriately press consistency without claiming that the analogies conclusively disprove resurrection.

charity.alternative: The resurrection evidence may have stronger source proximity, multiplicity, or historical support than the comparison cases.
charity.decisiveQualification: An analogy has force only after comparing the reliability and independence of each evidential record.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The consistency challenge is coherent, although rejection of other miracle claims does not alone entail rejection of this one.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete religious comparisons are supplied, but evidential comparability, dates, sources, and independence are not established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the subsidiary burden concerning discriminatory reliability of ancient miracle testimony.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move raises a fair parity demand but does not examine the strongest claimed distinctions in the Christian case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares resurrection belief with Mormon certificates, Muhammad's ascent, and other religious commitments through rhetorical parity questions.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Extensive suffering is logically incompatible with an omnipotent and benevolent God because such a being would eliminate suffering.
moves.attributionBasis: Rosenberg is still the continuously identified speaker, and he explicitly formulates the argument from evil while anticipating Craig's response.

response.rationale: This constructive claims a logical incompatibility between severe suffering and an omnipotent, benevolent God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The central incompatibility is stated plainly, but the necessity premise about benevolence is insufficiently qualified.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogism is recoverable, but 'benevolent' shifts toward an exceptionless duty to eliminate suffering without a stated condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Logical incompatibility requires excluding morally sufficient reasons, which the simple premise in the excerpt does not accomplish.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument depends on an unsupported universal premise that every benevolent omnipotent being eliminates all suffering.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The existence of suffering is uncontroversial here, but the decisive moral necessity connecting benevolence to elimination is asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the central con bridge alleging incompatibility between divine attributes and suffering.

representationalCharity.rationale: As a constructive, the selected span does not yet develop a specific theistic greater-good or freedom alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly formulates the argument from evil and states that a benevolent creature eliminates suffering.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The logical problem of evil requires excluding the possibility that God has morally sufficient reasons for permitting suffering.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly announces Craig's rebuttal immediately before this passage, and Craig directly addresses Rosenberg throughout the continuous span.

components.text: Identifies the missing necessity premise: the argument must exclude every possible morally sufficient divine reason.
Does not itself identify and substantiate a particular morally sufficient reason for the actual pattern of suffering.

response.rationale: The reply correctly states why Rosenberg's simple premises do not establish logical incompatibility and specifies the defeating burden, though it does not provide a positive theodicy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly diagnoses the decisive modal gap and states that the logical conclusion therefore does not follow.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply carefully limits its conclusion to failure of the logical version unless possible sufficient reasons are excluded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modal burden stated is appropriate for a logical-incompatibility claim and is not presented as proving a full theodicy.

charity.alternative: The amount and distribution of suffering may still provide a strong evidential argument even without strict contradiction.
charity.decisiveQualification: Defeating logical incompatibility does not defeat a probabilistic or evidential problem of evil.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response identifies the exact modal omission and correctly explains why the asserted contradiction has not been derived.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The logical point is well warranted internally, although the appeal to broad rejection is supplementary authority rather than needed support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central con incompatibility bridge and supports the corresponding pro coherence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response accurately targets Rosenberg's expressly logical claim, though its rhetoric briefly risks sounding broader than that limited defeat.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says Rosenberg must show that morally sufficient reasons are impossible and limits the criticism to the logical argument.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Metaphysical naturalism conflicts with reason and experience by denying intentionality, meaning, freedom, persistence, and persons.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage continues Craig's explicitly framed rebuttal and maintains his first-person argumentative voice throughout.

components.text: Challenges Rosenberg's broader naturalistic framework by arguing that denial of persons and first-person perspectives conflicts with certain experience.
Does not answer the Euthyphro grounding dilemma or defend objective morality's dependence on God.

response.rationale: The move supplies a substantive contrary argument against Rosenberg's naturalism, but it does not answer the decisive moral-grounding challenge in its legal earlier target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The material is relevant to Rosenberg's worldview but is a nonanswer to the targeted moral dilemma.

precisionFindings.rationale: The experiential reductio is clear, but naturalism, Rosenberg's eliminativism, and atheism are treated too interchangeably.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Certainty that persons exist may challenge eliminativism, but it does not establish that every metaphysical naturalism is false.

charity.alternative: Naturalists may retain persons and intentionality through non-eliminativist physicalist or emergent accounts.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reductio applies most directly to Rosenberg's stated eliminativism, not naturalism in every form.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The first-person reductio pressures eliminativism, while the universal conclusion about metaphysical naturalism commits a scope overreach.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First-person experience supports the immediate premise, but exclusion of rival naturalistic accounts is not supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally attacks a proposed naturalistic alternative, despite failing to answer the selected moral target.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument uses Rosenberg's strongest provocative consequences but generalizes them beyond the particular view defended.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt infers naturalism's falsity from the certainty of personal existence and contrasts metaphysical with epistemological naturalism.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Quantum-vacuum events do not establish emergence from nothing, and their causelessness remains disputed, so they do not defeat a causal inference from an absolute cosmic beginning.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces Rosenberg's response and answers it continuously in the established rebuttal turn.

components.text: Identifies that virtual particles arise from a physical quantum vacuum rather than from nothing.
Challenges the assertion of causelessness by noting that deterministic interpretations of quantum mechanics remain available.

response.rationale: The reply separates intra-vacuum events from absolute origination and identifies interpretive underdetermination, directly limiting both components of the quantum counterexample.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly diagnoses the analogy and interpretation defects and states their consequence for the causal inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between nothing and a quantum vacuum is stable, and uncertainty about causeless interpretations is expressly acknowledged.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately argues that the counterexample is not decisive rather than claiming all quantum events have causes.

charity.alternative: Radioactive decay, rather than virtual-particle emergence, may still challenge a universal sufficient-cause principle.
charity.decisiveQualification: The vacuum distinction answers emergence-from-nothing language but does not alone settle every quantum counterexample.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The two-part answer coherently distinguishes physical background conditions and denies that one indeterministic reading is compulsory.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The vacuum's physical character and interpretive plurality are specific supports, though no further defense of the interpretations appears.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central naturalistic-alternatives bridge as applied to cosmic causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response handles the strongest interpretation fairly and adds the relevant interpretive qualification, with a bounded scope gap.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that virtual particles arise from a quantum vacuum and notes deterministic interpretations of quantum mechanics.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Atheism and the disputed philosophical doctrines are parallel implications attributed to science, so rejecting those doctrines does not logically refute atheism.
moves.attributionBasis: Rosenberg is explicitly introduced at the start of the turn and identifies his own book and its argumentative structure.

components.text: Identifies that disputing Rosenberg's additional philosophical doctrines does not logically refute atheism.
Does not provide a positive naturalistic account of intentional mental states or aboutness.

response.rationale: The reply correctly exposes the scope error from attacking Rosenberg's doctrines to refuting atheism, while leaving Craig's underlying intentionality datum unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly defeats the overbroad inference but only partially addresses the larger mind argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between atheism and Rosenberg's controversial philosophical theses is expressed clearly and consistently.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical point is appropriately categorical: controverting parallel theses does not by itself controvert atheism.

charity.alternative: Craig may be targeting Rosenberg's specific scientific naturalism rather than every possible atheism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig's excerpt expressly broadens the conclusion to naturalism and atheism, making the scope objection materially applicable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parallel-implication distinction directly blocks the alleged reductio unless an additional entailment from atheism is supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The logical separation is well supported by the stated argumentative structure, though the claimed relation to science is not independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks Craig's central use of intentionality against the naturalistic side, though it offers no replacement account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the actual inference at issue and fairly separates the debate motion from Rosenberg's broader doctrines.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the disputed doctrines are parallel philosophical implications and that refuting them does not refute atheism.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Creaturely freedom limits which worlds God can actualize, and humans cannot establish that comparable goods, salvation, and knowledge of God were feasible with less evil.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Craig the floor, and Craig directly addresses Rosenberg by name and answers his final challenge.

components.text: Contacts logical incompatibility by arguing that creaturely freedom constrains which good worlds are feasible for God.
Challenges the claim that an equally good world with less evil was feasible by placing the proof burden on that modal assertion.

response.rationale: The reply supplies a freedom-based possibility and attacks the unproved feasible-world premise, which is enough against strict logical incompatibility but not a complete evidential theodicy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Both decisive logical components are contacted explicitly, with the conclusion properly aimed at impossibility proof.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently concerns feasible worlds and the limited burden of defeating a logical, rather than evidential, argument.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The burden critique is sound, although saying the contrary is impossible to prove is stronger than merely noting it has not been proved.

charity.alternative: An omnipotent God might create free agents who always freely choose well or prevent extreme suffering without removing freedom.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defense must distinguish logically possible worlds from worlds feasible given creaturely counterfactuals and other goods.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The modal defense coherently blocks contradiction, though it does not independently establish the asserted constraints on feasible worlds.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The response names freedom, salvation, and knowledge of God, but their necessity for the actual suffering remains speculative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central pro bridge reconciling divine goodness, power, freedom, and suffering.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move engages the feasible-world demand but relies substantially on epistemic limitation rather than a fully developed feasibility account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies that Rosenberg can establish a comparable feasible world with less evil and ties this to rejection of the logical problem.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Uncaused alpha decay and quantum symmetry breaking undermine the assumption that the universe's earliest state must have a sufficient cause.
moves.attributionBasis: Rosenberg is explicitly identified at the beginning of the uninterrupted rebuttal and formulates the challenge in his own voice.

components.text: Contacts the cosmic distinction by relying on radioactive decay and symmetry breaking rather than only virtual particles from a vacuum.
Extends the quantum analogy directly to the assumption that the universe's earliest state requires a cause.

response.rationale: The reply avoids part of the virtual-particle objection and expressly asks why cosmic quantum processes differ, but the cross-scale analogy remains asserted rather than demonstrated.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts both the vacuum reply and original causal premise, though it does not resolve their crucial scope distinction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The examples are identifiable, but 'without a cause' and extension from local quantum processes to the whole universe remain unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move treats one interpretation and a cosmic analogy as established despite unresolved interpretive and scope questions.

charity.alternative: The universe's absolute beginning may differ categorically from fluctuations or symmetry breaking within an existing physical state.
charity.decisiveQualification: A valid counterexample requires showing that the relevant causal principle and ontological conditions are genuinely parallel.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy creates a legitimate challenge to universality, but the conclusion requires an unargued transfer from intra-universe physics.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete quantum phenomena are named, while their causeless interpretation and relevance to the initial cosmic state are asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central naturalistic-alternatives bridge against cosmic causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The rhetorical question recognizes the needed comparison but does not engage the strongest claimed difference between local events and absolute origination.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes alpha decay and quantum symmetry breaking and expressly asks why the universe should be assumed different.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Freedom does not require catastrophic wrongdoing because God could create free agents who always choose rightly or never face suffering-producing circumstances.
moves.attributionBasis: The argument is delivered continuously by Rosenberg in his identified rebuttal, with explicit references to Craig's free-will defense.

components.text: Contacts the feasibility claim by proposing free agents who always choose rightly or are not exposed to destructive temptation.
Challenges freedom as a morally sufficient reason for catastrophic suffering but does not exclude every possible sufficient reason.

response.rationale: The reply directly tests whether freedom requires actual grave wrongdoing and offers alternative arrangements, but it assumes rather than proves that such worlds are feasible.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive freedom component and substantially addresses the sufficient-reason defense.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed alternatives are clear, with feasibility and the distinction between choosing rightly and determined conduct left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The repeated questions appropriately present a live possibility rather than claiming a demonstrated feasible world.

charity.alternative: A world where free creatures always choose rightly may be possible but not feasible for God to actualize with those creatures.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection must address the counterfactuals of creaturely freedom rather than only describe a logically conceivable outcome.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternatives show that freedom and suffering are not conceptually identical, though feasibility remains a material missing bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The classroom analogy and proposed worlds illuminate the issue but cannot establish divine feasibility or comparable goods.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central pro evil-coherence bridge and supports the con incompatibility route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move sharply identifies the intuitive challenge but does not fully meet the specialized feasibility qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks why free agents could not always choose rightly or avoid temptation while retaining free will.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: God lacks the predictive contribution that warrants accepting theoretical entities in science and therefore does not qualify as a reasonable scientific hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Rosenberg's closing statement, and Rosenberg explicitly presents this passage as a positive argument for atheism.

components.text: Contacts the design inference by arguing that God adds no predictive contribution warranting scientific explanatory acceptance.
Extends the no-prediction criticism to divine explanation generally without separately analyzing cosmological explanatory content.

response.rationale: The move gives a clear methodological objection to accepting God as a scientific hypothesis, but it assumes prediction is indispensable rather than addressing nonpredictive theoretical virtues.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the design inference directly and broader divine explanation, with one decisive standards premise left undefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The predictive criterion is clear, but the conclusion shifts from use in science to explanatory or rational use without qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: No scientific predictive role may limit scientific utility, but it does not establish no explanatory basis of any kind.

charity.alternative: Explanatory power, simplicity, unification, and fit with background knowledge can support hypotheses without novel predictions.
charity.decisiveQualification: The no-need argument requires either showing prediction is necessary or showing God lacks the other theoretical virtues too.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from no predictive contribution to no explanatory basis depends on an unsupported necessary-condition premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological assertion and Laplace example are specific, but no representative defense of predictive indispensability is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central con bridge challenging divine explanatory content.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Cross-cultural norms of fairness, equality, reciprocity, and cooperation can arise through natural selection because they enhanced human survival.
moves.attributionBasis: An explicit Dr. Rosenberg label introduces the answer, which remains an uninterrupted response in his characteristic first-person framing.

components.text: Contacts the claimed explanatory gap by offering natural selection as an account of shared cooperative moral norms.
Does not explain objective normativity or show why evolved dispositions are genuinely morally right.
Provides a positive naturalistic account in one domain but does not address intentionality or persons.

response.rationale: The evolutionary story answers the origin and commonality of moral practices, but it does not contact the distinct grounding demand concerning objective truth or obligation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts an important explanatory component while leaving the decisive normative-grounding component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evolutionary claim is clear, but moral norms, cooperative dispositions, and objective moral truths are not sharply distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move frames natural selection as an explanatory answer to commonality without expressly claiming that evolution establishes objective rightness.

charity.alternative: Evolution may explain moral beliefs and cooperation while leaving their objective truth or authority unexplained.
charity.decisiveQualification: A genealogical account of dispositions is not by itself an ontological ground for moral facts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Selection for cooperation plausibly explains common norms, though any inference to objective morality would be a category shift.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Fairness, equality, reciprocity, and cooperation are representative mechanisms, but supporting evolutionary detail is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally supplies a naturalistic alternative for moral practices, even though it does not defeat objective grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reframed question is legitimate and well motivated, but it does not replace the original objective-grounding demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt reframes cross-cultural moral commonality and identifies cooperation, fairness, equality, and reciprocity as selection-shaped traits.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Moral values are grounded non-arbitrarily in God's essentially good character, while duties arise through commands that express that character.
moves.attributionBasis: An explicit Dr. Craig label starts the passage, and his answer continues without any intervening change of speaker.

components.text: Contacts arbitrariness by grounding goodness in God's essential character rather than unconstrained divine will.
Explains duties as commands reflecting that character, but does not independently justify identifying God's nature with goodness.
Does not contest the evolutionary account of cooperative dispositions or distinguish it empirically.

response.rationale: The response directly presents the standard nature-based answer to voluntarism and connects commands to character, while leaving the deeper identity claim largely stipulated.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts both arbitrariness and command components, with the ultimate goodness-grounding bridge compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction among will, character, values, and duties is stated clearly and consistently.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents a coherent mainstream alternative to voluntarism without claiming that the short answer conclusively proves it.

charity.alternative: Calling God the paradigm of goodness may relocate rather than solve the grounding question.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account still must explain the content and noncircular authority of the claimed essentially good nature.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The nature-based structure avoids the simple Euthyphro horn, though the identity between God and goodness remains underargued.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual account is specific, but its central metaphysical identification is asserted rather than independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the subsidiary con burden challenging divine moral grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly distinguishes its position from crude command voluntarism but does not fully resolve the strongest residual challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects voluntarism, identifies God as the paradigm of goodness, and treats commands as reflections of divine character.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Predictive novelty is not the sole test of a hypothesis because explanatory power, simplicity, plausibility, and other theoretical virtues can also support theism.
moves.attributionBasis: A Dr. Craig label explicitly introduces the extended answer, which remains his uninterrupted response through its concluding comparison with atheism.

components.text: Identifies that predictability is not a necessary test when empirically equivalent theories differ.
Supplies simplicity, plausibility, ad hocness, and explanatory power as additional standards.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects the purported necessity of prediction and provides recognized replacement criteria, though it does not demonstrate that theism performs well on each criterion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly diagnoses the standards error and answers it with multiple relevant theoretical virtues.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that prediction is not the sole criterion follows from the empirically equivalent-theory example if that example is accepted.

charity.alternative: Prediction may remain especially important even if not literally the only theoretical virtue.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting exclusivity does not establish that explanatory virtues can compensate for weak empirical constraint in every case.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample and list of alternative virtues coherently refute the sole-criterion claim, with one bounded application gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Empirical equivalence provides a specific methodological example, though theism's actual comparative performance is not shown here.

moves.speaker: Alex Rosenberg
moves.proposition: Denying intrinsic meaning and intentionality is not self-refuting because sounds, marks, and pixels can transmit information by causally reorganizing neural circuits.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage begins with an explicit Dr. Rosenberg label and remains his uninterrupted reading and explanation until the audience applause.

components.text: Contacts the self-refutation challenge by explaining communication as causal transmission that reorganizes neural circuits.
Addresses the apparent inconsistency of publishing claims while denying intrinsic statement content.
Does not bear on explanatory virtues or predictive standards.

response.rationale: The reply offers a causal-information model that answers how discourse can function without intrinsic aboutness, but it does not fully explain truth, reference, or why the content is determinate.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive self-refutation component and provides a mechanism, with semantic adequacy unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal proposal is recoverable, but 'information' risks reintroducing the semantic notion that the argument denies unless defined nonsemantically.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The model plausibly explains causal influence, but the excerpt treats that as sufficient for communication despite the residual semantic problem.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Sounds, marks, pixels, and neural rearrangement provide a concrete mechanism, while semantic sufficiency is not established.
